entry.title: Making a Diffusion Model Forget, Without the Training Data

link.title: Making a Diffusion Model Forget, Without the Training Data

entry.content:
Problem. Diffusion models can generate content you need to remove after training, such as a class or an artist’s style. Retraining without that data is expensive, and most unlearning methods assume access to the full training set.
Approach. A one-step, data-constrained method that fine-tunes the model using only the data to be forgotten, with a loss derived from variational inference.
Result. High unlearning rates with far better image quality than the baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and tinyImageNet, and style and object removal in Stable Diffusion. Published in TMLR 2026.

Suppose you have a trained diffusion model and you find out it can produce something it shouldn’t: a copyrighted artist’s style, a person’s likeness, or just a class you no longer want it to generate. The clean fix is to retrain from scratch without that data. That is usually far too expensive, and often impossible, because you no longer have the full training set.

This post walks through Variational Diffusion Unlearning (VDU), the method we developed during my research internship in Prof. Prathosh A.P.’s lab at IISc Bangalore. It started as a NeurIPS 2024 workshop paper (Safe Generative AI) and grew into a journal paper in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2026), with Subhodip Panda, M S Varun, Sarthak Kumar Maharana and Prathosh A.P.

The setting: you only have what you want to forget

Most unlearning methods for diffusion models quietly assume you still have the data you want to keep. Selective Amnesia replays generated samples of the remaining classes. Saliency Unlearning (SalUn) perturbs the most influential weights using the whole training set as a reference. That is reasonable in a lab, but in practice the full training set is often gone, private, or far too large to touch.

So we set a stricter rule. The only data available is \(D_f\), a small set of images showing the thing to forget. The remaining data \(D_r\) is off-limits. Under that rule, the obvious approach fails badly: if you simply push the model’s likelihood down on \(D_f\), it does forget, but it also forgets how to make good images of anything. This is catastrophic forgetting, and in this setting there is no remaining data to anchor the model.

The question becomes: can we forget \(D_f\) while keeping generation quality, using nothing but \(D_f\) and the pretrained weights?

Unlearning as Bayesian bookkeeping

The key move is to think about the weights as a distribution rather than a single point.

A model trained on everything is a sample from the posterior \(P(\theta \mid D_r, D_f)\). The model we wish we had, retrained without \(D_f\), is a sample from \(P(\theta \mid D_r)\). Bayes’ rule links the two, because the data points are independent:

\[P(\theta \mid D_r) \;\propto\; \frac{P(\theta \mid D_r, D_f)}{P(D_f \mid \theta)}\]

In words: start from the full posterior and divide out the evidence that came from the forget set. We never need \(D_r\) directly. We only need the full-data posterior, which the pretrained model gives us, and the likelihood of \(D_f\), which we can compute.

That target is intractable, so we approximate it with a simpler distribution \(Q(\theta)\) by minimising a KL divergence, the standard variational inference recipe:

\[Q^*(\theta) = \arg\min_{Q} \; D_{KL}\!\left(Q(\theta) \,\Big\|\, Z \cdot \frac{P(\theta \mid D_f, D_r)}{P(D_f \mid \theta)}\right)\]

With a Gaussian mean-field assumption on the weights, and the diffusion model’s usual variational bound on log-likelihood, this works out to a loss with two parts.

The loss: a push and a leash

\[\mathcal{L}_{VDU} = \underbrace{-(1-\gamma)\,\mathbb{E}_{x_0 \sim D_f,\,\epsilon,\,t}\!\left[w_t \,\big\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\big\|^2\right]}_{\text{plasticity inducer}} \;+\; \underbrace{\gamma \sum_{i=1}^{d} \frac{(\theta_i - \mu^*_i)^2}{2\sigma^{*2}_i}}_{\text{stability regularizer}}\]
  • The plasticity inducer is the push. It is the ordinary denoising loss on the forget set, with the sign flipped. Minimising it makes the model worse at denoising images of the unwanted class, so it stops producing them.
  • The stability regularizer is the leash. Each weight is pulled back towards its pretrained mean \(\mu^*_i\), scaled by \(1/\sigma^{*2}_i\). Weights the model is confident about (small variance) are held tightly; uncertain ones are free to move.
  • \(\gamma\) sets the balance between forgetting and staying put.

This looks like Elastic Weight Consolidation, which Selective Amnesia uses, but it comes from a different place and is cheaper. EWC weights its penalty with the Fisher information matrix, which needs gradient products over data. VDU gets \(\mu^*\) and \(\sigma^*\) directly from the spread of the weights across independently trained checkpoints: we trained five models per dataset and used their per-weight mean and variance. Once those are in hand, unlearning is a plain fine-tuning loop on \(D_f\), usually for a single epoch.

Does it work?

We tested two kinds of forgetting:

  • Class unlearning: removing a class (a digit, “ship”, “fish”, “butcher shop”) from unconditional DDPMs trained on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and tinyImageNet.
  • Feature unlearning: removing a concept such as Van Gogh’s style or cars from Stable Diffusion, pretrained on LAION-5B.

Two numbers matter. PUL (percentage of unlearning) counts how many fewer unwanted samples the model generates afterwards, judged by a classifier over 5,000 samples; higher is better. u-FID measures the quality of everything else the model still generates; lower is better. A method that wins only one of these isn’t useful: you can get 100% PUL by breaking the model.

All baselines were held to the same rule (no access to \(D_r\)) and the same short compute budget. “Fine-tuning” is a reference point that does see \(D_r\), so it shows roughly the best you could hope for.

Dataset Forgotten class Fine-tuning (sees \(D_r\)) SA SalUn ESD VDU
MNIST Digit 1 90.1 / 5.9 15.0 / 301.3 45.3 / 68.8 56.7 / 66.2 75.1 / 14.4
MNIST Digit 8 94.3 / 6.2 49.0 / 161.1 32.5 / 50.2 32.7 / 55.7 69.0 / 38.2
CIFAR-10 Automobile 88.0 / 9.0 2.3 / 92.9 12.0 / 66.5 9.0 / 73.5 60.9 / 30.9
CIFAR-10 Ship 92.9 / 10.7 85.0 / 249.9 55.1 / 75.5 58.3 / 77.1 71.6 / 24.5
tinyImageNet Fish 82.6 / 13.8 67.7 / 32.0 39.3 / 42.7 41.7 / 45.2 58.8 / 29.9
tinyImageNet Butcher shop 83.4 / 16.8 6.7 / 24.0 2.9 / 33.5 8.8 / 39.5 66.7 / 24.2

Each cell is PUL (%) / u-FID, averaged over three seeds.

The pattern is consistent. Among methods that respect the no-\(D_r\) rule, VDU has the best image quality on every class, and the best or near-best forgetting. Where a baseline forgets more, it pays dearly for it. Selective Amnesia removes 85% of ships from CIFAR-10, but its u-FID of 250 means the rest of its output has collapsed. VDU removes 72% with a u-FID of 24.5, roughly ten times better.

It is also fast. VDU needed one epoch on MNIST and two on tinyImageNet, while SalUn and ESD needed five on every dataset.

Forgetting a style in Stable Diffusion

The same loss scales to Stable Diffusion. Here the “forget set” is a handful of images showing the concept, and we watch what the model produces for a fixed prompt and seed as unlearning goes on.

These grids also show the method’s central trade-off. Every extra epoch of the plasticity inducer removes more of the concept, but also drifts the weights further from the original model.

The trade-off in numbers

That trade-off is clear in the epoch ablation. Unlearning digit 1 from MNIST:

Epochs 1 2 3 4 5
PUL (%) 75.1 86.6 97.9 99.6 100.0
u-FID 14.4 33.7 56.2 106.2 218.8

By epoch 5 the digit is completely gone, but image quality is 15 times worse. The reason is built into the loss: the plasticity term has no lower bound, so if you keep minimising it, the model keeps moving away from where it started. In practice you stop early, after one or two epochs, where most of the forgetting has happened and quality is still close to the original.

\(\gamma\) is the other control. At \(\gamma = 1\) only the leash is active, so the model barely changes (PUL of 17% on MNIST, under 2% on CIFAR-10). At \(\gamma = 0\) there is no leash. Values between 0.1 and 0.3 gave the best balance across datasets.

Limitations

  • Gaussian mean-field weights. This is what makes the loss simple, but real weight posteriors are correlated and not Gaussian. A richer posterior could help.
  • You need several checkpoints. \(\mu^*\) and \(\sigma^*\) come from independently trained models. That is cheap for small DDPMs but not for a model the size of Stable Diffusion, unless the checkpoints already exist.
  • No natural stopping point. Because the plasticity term is unbounded, the number of epochs is a real hyperparameter that needs tuning.

Takeaway

The idea I find most satisfying here is the reframing: unlearning isn’t “do gradient ascent and hope”. Write down which posterior you actually want, see that Bayes’ rule lets you reach it without the data you’ve lost, and let variational inference turn that into a loss. The two resulting terms, a push away from the forget set and a variance-weighted leash back to the original, explain both why the method works and where it breaks.

Links: TMLR paper (OpenReview) · arXiv

My role

  • Worked on the variational formulation and the stability regularizer as a research intern (May–Nov 2024).
  • Ran class-unlearning experiments on DDPMs and the comparisons with the baselines.
  • Co-authored the NeurIPS 2024 Safe Generative AI workshop paper and the TMLR journal version.

entry.title: How we won silver at Inter-IIT 14.0 with 1/5th the compute

link.title: How we won silver at Inter-IIT 14.0 with 1/5th the compute

entry.content:
Problem. ISRO’s Inter-IIT 14.0 problem asked for a natural-language interface to Earth-observation imagery: captioning, visual question answering (VQA) and oriented referring-expression grounding, over RGB, false-colour (FCC) and SAR inputs, using only open-source models that run offline.
Approach. A neuro-symbolic Refine-Generate-Filter-Reason pipeline: deterministic domain adaptation to a unified RGB, a fine-tuned SAM3 for oriented grounding, CLIP and NMS filtering, a VLM for final selection, and a router that sends numeric questions to a geometry engine.
Result. 31.3% Acc@0.7 for grounding on VRSBench (GeoChat: 19.9%). Silver Medal, second place on the leaderboard with 320.13 points behind IIT Delhi’s 400.
My role. Team lead. I assembled the team, set the technical direction for every vertical, managed budget and GPU compute, and presented to the judges. I personally drove the SAM3-based grounding pipeline.

In December 2025 our six-person team (Team 58: Karan Gandhi, Laksh Jain, Romit Mohane, Shreyans Jain, Umang Shikarvar and Viraj Vekaria) took the Silver Medal on the ISRO problem statement at Inter-IIT Tech Meet 14.0. We finished second, with 320.13 points behind IIT Delhi’s 400, and we did it using less than one-fifth of the compute the other top-5 teams used. Their budgets were roughly ₹1-2 lakh.

I was the team lead. This post is the leadership and strategy story: how I picked the team, how we chose a direction, where we spent and did not spend compute, and what failed. The full technical details are in the last section, and the code is at Umang-Shikarvar/GeoNLI.

The brief

ISRO wanted one natural-language interface to Earth-observation imagery. It had to caption a scene, answer questions (yes/no, numeric, or free-form) and ground a referring expression such as “the smallest plane near the vehicle” with an oriented box. Inputs could be RGB, false-colour composite (FCC) or SAR, and the whole thing had to run on open-source models offline.

That is three tasks, three modalities and one deployment constraint, so the first job as lead was not choosing a model. It was deciding how the work would be split so that every piece fit into the same system.

Building the team and splitting the work

I selected and assembled the six of us, then set the technical direction for each vertical: captioning, VQA, grounding, domain adaptation and the UI. The split mattered because the tasks depend on each other. Captions use grounding output as input, numeric VQA uses grounding output, and every task depends on getting non-RGB images into a form the models understand. If each person had built a standalone solution, we would have had six demos and no system.

I kept grounding for myself. It was the task everything else leaned on, so it was the one where a mistake would cost us the most, and I wanted to be the person debugging it.

How we chose a direction

The report lays out why off-the-shelf VLMs struggle here, and these reasons drove the plan:

  • Coordinates as tokens lose precision. A VLM that emits box coordinates quantises them into bins. In a parking lot or a harbour full of containers, neighbouring objects merge.
  • Axis-aligned bias. A ship lying on a diagonal gets a box full of background.
  • Hallucinated arithmetic. VLMs miscount dense clusters and cannot compute area or perimeter.
  • Spectral mismatch. FCC and SAR images do not look like what RGB-trained encoders were trained on. Passing FCC directly led to errors like reading red vegetation as fire.

Each problem pointed at the same idea: do not ask one end-to-end model to do everything. Let each component do what it is good at, and put deterministic code wherever a precise answer exists. That gave us the neuro-symbolic structure: fix the input first, ground with a segmentation model, filter and reason over candidates, and compute numbers instead of guessing them.

Why segmentation-first grounding

This was the central bet, and I drove it. Instead of asking a VLM for coordinates, we ask SAM3 for masks and recover oriented boxes from the contours with rotating calipers. That solves the precision, merging and rotation problems together.

SAM3 on its own over-segments, though. On an airport scene it returns shadows, gangways and service vehicles as “airplanes”. So the pipeline has four stages:

  1. Refine. Mistral-7B strips spatial language from the query (“leftmost airplane” becomes “airplane”), because a segmenter has no idea what “leftmost” means.
  2. Generate. A SAM3 model fine-tuned on VRSBench produces dense masks and oriented boxes.
  3. Filter. CLIP scores each rotated crop against the class text, and NMS removes duplicates.
  4. Reason. Qwen3-VL sees the image with indexed, coloured boxes and picks the ones matching the full query, returning JSON with a rationale.

The point of the last stage is a division of labour. A VLM is poor at regressing coordinates but good at looking at five numbered boxes and saying which one is “the smallest plane”. We turned a hard task into an easy one.

Fine-tuning on sparse labels

VRSBench does not label every instance. The report gives the example of 5 of 50 cars being annotated. A detector trained to find everything gets penalised for correct detections that nobody labelled. So we trained SAM3 on the single instance a query refers to, with a weakly supervised setup, and a composite loss of focal, presence, L1 and GIoU terms.

Compute: where we spent and where we did not

The headline number is the budget. The other top-5 teams were working with budgets of roughly ₹1-2 lakh, and we used less than a fifth of the compute they did. I managed the budget and the GPU allocation, so I can say what that looked like in the design.

The report does not give a per-decision cost breakdown, so I will stick to the choices it documents, which all point the same way:

  • No training of large models from scratch. Everything is built on open-source models used zero-shot or lightly adapted. Domain adaptation is a deterministic layer, a linear model for FCC, so RGB-pretrained models work unchanged.
  • Small, cheap fine-tuning. SAM3 was trained with frozen vision and text encoders, updating only the mask decoder and prompt encoder, for a single epoch. Captioning used LoRA with mixed precision on a single A100. VQA fine-tuning used two L40S GPUs.
  • Deterministic code instead of more model. Counting, length, area and perimeter come from geometry on the filtered boxes. A larger model would have cost more and still guessed.
  • Selective use of expensive steps. Super-resolution helped attribute recognition on very low-resolution crops but sometimes added artefacts, so we used it selectively rather than everywhere.

The lesson I took from it: compute efficiency is mostly an architecture decision. Every time a deterministic component can replace a model call, you save GPU time and gain debuggability.

What failed or nearly did

The ablations in the report are a decent record of the things that went wrong:

  • Removing the CLIP filter caused a spike in false positives, mostly shadows, and IoU dropped by about 12%.
  • Fine-tuning the full SAM3 diverged after two epochs. Freezing the vision encoder was essential.
  • Aggressive loss weights were unstable. Lowering the classification and presence weights from 20 to 10 and the focal positive weight from 10 to 5 helped, with gradient clipping and warmup. Cutting the focal weight all the way from 20 to 1 made the model ignore small objects entirely.
  • More epochs overfit and hurt zero-shot generalisation. One epoch was best out of the 1-5 we tried.

None of these was a surprise in hindsight, but each one cost iteration time, which is exactly what a budget-constrained team cannot waste.

VQA and captioning: letting the pipeline do the hard part

Captioning is grounding-first. We serialise the verified detections into the prompt and tell the model to use only those, which cuts hallucinated objects. The cost is a recall ceiling: if SAM3 misses an object, the caption cannot mention it.

VQA uses a Mistral-7B router. Semantic questions go to a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B, while binary and numeric ones go through grounding. For numbers, a geometry engine computes the answer. The fine-tuned VLM alone scored 90.86 binary accuracy but only 0.56 on the numeric score, which is why the engine exists. If anything fails to parse, the system falls back to the VLM so an answer always comes back.

The result, honestly

On the VRSBench validation split, strict grounding accuracy (Acc@0.7) was 31.3% against 19.9% for GeoChat and 13.6% for LLaVA-1.5. On the crowded non-unique subset it was 32.5% against 18.0% for GeoChat. GeoChat still beats us on Unique Acc@0.5 (57.4 vs 52.5), so the win is about precision and clutter. In captioning we lead on BLEU-1 (52.9) and report BERTScore F1 0.897, but trail on BLEU-2 to BLEU-4 because our captions are terse.

Presenting it

I led the final presentation to the judges. The pipeline’s stage-by-stage structure helped here: it is easy to show a dense airport scene and walk through raw SAM3 output, NMS, CLIP filtering and the final selection. Explainability was a real asset when time was short.

What I would do differently

  • Errors cascade. A hierarchical pipeline is explainable, but its recall ceiling is set by the first stage.
  • The router is fragile. It can misroute ambiguous queries, and malformed VLM JSON can still slip past regex extraction and repair.
  • Geometry assumptions. Rotating calipers assume convex shapes, so U-shaped buildings get loose boxes.
  • Generated inputs. Pix2Pix can invent or erase structure in SAR, and fixed FCC coefficients may shift colours on uncalibrated sensors.

The biggest lesson was about leadership as much as modelling: pick one architectural idea, make every vertical serve it, and spend compute only where a model is genuinely needed.

The code is on GitHub.

Technical details

The story above covers the decisions. This section is the reference: the full architecture, the remaining pipeline pieces and every number from the report.

System overview

Domain adaptation

A deterministic layer converts every input to RGB so that RGB-pretrained models work zero-shot. FCC images are converted to natural colour by synthesising the missing blue channel with a linear model over green, red and NIR (following Patra et al.), which avoids errors like reading red vegetation as fire. SAR images go through a Pix2Pix SAR-to-RGB generator. Real-ESRGAN is used only as a 4x sharpening step so small objects keep clean edges.

Query types

Full results

All numbers are on the official VRSBench validation split (9,350 images).

Method Unique @0.5 Unique @0.7 Non-Unique @0.5 Non-Unique @0.7 All @0.5 All @0.7
GeoChat w/o ft 20.7 5.4 7.3 1.7 12.9 3.2
LLaVA-1.5 51.1 16.4 34.8 11.5 41.6 13.6
GeoChat 57.4 22.6 44.5 18.0 49.8 19.9
GeoNLI 52.5 30.0 55.0 32.5 53.8 31.3

Strict-precision accuracy (Acc@0.7) is about double the strong VLM baselines, and the gain is largest on the non-unique (crowded) subset: 32.5% against 18.0% for GeoChat. GeoChat still wins the loose Unique Acc@0.5, so the advantage is precision and clutter handling, not everywhere.

Unique 42.60%
Non-Unique 42.28%
Overall 42.44%

VQA (fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B baseline, without the router pipeline):

Semantic (BERT-BLEU) 0.79

MAE / RMSE 0.73 / 1.41

The 0.56 numeric score is why the deterministic engine exists: it replaces estimation with calculation. The report does not give separate numbers for the full hybrid pipeline.

Captioning:

GeoChat w/o ft 13.9 6.6 3.0 1.4 0.4 -

GeoNLI leads on BLEU-1 but trails on BLEU-2 to BLEU-4, which the report attributes to a concise captioning style. CIDEr was not reported for our model.

Ablations.

  • Removing the CLIP filter dropped IoU by about 12%, mostly from SAM3 segmenting shadows.
  • Fine-tuning the full SAM3 diverged after two epochs; freezing the vision encoder was essential.
  • Cutting the focal loss weight from 20 to 1 made the model ignore small objects entirely.
  • One epoch was best; further training overfit and hurt zero-shot generalisation.

Demo and UI

A React (Vite) dashboard sits in front of a Flask GPU backend, with a Vercel proxy providing an HTTPS endpoint for judge evaluation. Users upload an image, pick its type (RGB, SAR or FCC) and spatial resolution, generate a caption, or chat with Grounding and VQA toggles to get text answers and OBB overlays. A single POST /geoNLI/eval endpoint serves a structured evaluation mode and an interactive mode, and models are pre-loaded at startup.

Stack: Flask, React + Vite, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers; Mistral-7B, Qwen3-VL, SAM 3, OpenCLIP, Pix2Pix, Real-ESRGAN.

entry.title: Mapping Blood Vessels from a Few Hundred Ultrasound Frames

link.title: Mapping Blood Vessels from a Few Hundred Ultrasound Frames

entry.content:
Problem. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) resolves vessels below 50 um, but needs ultrafast frame rates (about 1000 FPS), tens of thousands of frames, and hours of processing, which clinical scanners cannot provide.
Approach. Skip bubble localization and tracking. A transformer-decoder network with learned linear projections maps a sparse low-frame-rate (2-50 FPS) contrast-enhanced sequence directly to a vessel probability map, followed by a post-processing enhancement stage.
Result. On in-vivo rat brain bolus data (PALA), vascular topology is recovered with up to 500x data reduction (341 frames at 2 FPS vs. 170,400 frames for ULM). End-to-end reconstruction takes 28-133 s on an NVIDIA H100. The cost is resolution: vessels appear about 3x wider.

Ultrasound is cheap, portable and safe, but it’s blurry. Its resolution is limited by diffraction to roughly half a wavelength, a few hundred microns at clinical frequencies, so the smallest vessels in an organ simply blur together. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) gets round this, and resolves vessels below 50 µm. But it asks for things a normal scanner can’t give.

This post is about VascFlexMap, a deep-learning method we’ve been developing at the MUSE Lab, IIT Gandhinagar (Prof. Himanshu Shekhar), with Ruchika Dhawan and Mihir Agarwal as equal-contribution first authors. The idea is to give up some of ULM’s resolution in exchange for working from the kind of sparse, slow data a clinical scanner can actually collect.

How ULM beats diffraction, and what it costs

ULM borrows its trick from optical super-resolution microscopy (PALM/STORM). You inject microbubbles, tiny gas-filled contrast agents that flow through the blood. Each bubble is far smaller than the ultrasound resolution, so it appears as a blurry spot. But if the bubbles are sparse enough that spots don’t overlap, you can find the centre of each spot far more precisely than its width. Record many frames, localize every bubble in every frame, track them from frame to frame, and add up all the tracks. The result is a map of where blood flows, at a resolution set by localization precision rather than diffraction.

The catch is in “many frames”:

  • Ultrafast imaging. Tracking needs bubbles to move only a little between frames, so ULM runs at about 1,000 frames per second, using plane-wave imaging that most clinical machines don’t offer.
  • Lots of data. Because bubbles must be sparse, each frame contributes only a few localizations. Filling in a vessel tree takes tens of thousands of frames: 170,400 in the rat-brain dataset we used.
  • Slow processing. Localization and tracking over that much data can take hours.

For many clinical questions (is this tissue perfused? where do the main branches run?) the network’s topology matters more than capillary-level detail. That’s the gap VascFlexMap targets.

The earlier step: a U-Net on sparse data

The project grew out of work we presented at ISTU 2024: a hybrid attention-based U-Net that reconstructs super-resolved vessel maps from sparse data. On simulated vessels, it cut the data needed by about 40× and improved peak SNR by 14.73 dB over ULM run on the same sparse data.

The middle panel shows the core problem. With too few frames, ULM has no tracks to accumulate, so it doesn’t degrade gracefully: it falls apart. A learned model, though, can use a prior about what vessel networks look like. VascFlexMap takes that idea to real in-vivo data.

VascFlexMap: skip localization altogether

Instead of finding bubbles and then drawing tracks, VascFlexMap maps a sparse sequence of frames directly to a vessel probability map.

Simulating a slow scanner

We used the public PALA rat-brain bolus dataset, recorded at 1,000 FPS. To simulate slower scanners, we kept every N-th frame of each 800-frame block, giving effective rates of 50, 25, 15, 5, 3 and 2 FPS. Tissue signal is removed with SVD clutter filtering: tissue moves slowly and coherently, so it lives in the first few singular vectors of the frame stack, while moving bubbles don’t. A second-order Butterworth band-pass then removes what’s left, and frames are resized to 256 × 256.

Learning a prior over vessel shapes

The most unusual design choice is in training. The network is trained with Gaussian-noise tensors as input, paired with full-data ULM vessel maps as targets. It doesn’t learn to read particular features from noisy frames; it learns a strong prior over what plausible vessel maps look like. We think this makes it less sensitive to things that change between scans (gain, attenuation, bubble concentration), and it converges in just 2 epochs.

The architecture

  • Each frame’s feature tensor (256 × 32 × 32, so 262,144 values) is linearly projected to 128 dimensions, so each frame becomes one token.
  • A 3-layer, single-head transformer encoder with sinusoidal positional encodings attends across the sequence. This is where information from many sparse frames is combined, much as ULM accumulates tracks over time.
  • A second projection restores the spatial tensor, and three transposed-convolution stages (256 → 128 → 64 → 32 channels) with a sigmoid output produce a 256 × 256 probability map.
  • Training uses binary cross-entropy and Adam at a learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴.

Cleaning up the output

The raw probability map is then enhanced: total-variation denoising, contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalisation (CLAHE), unsharp masking and a small erosion to thin the vessels, followed by 32× upscaling for display.

Results

How low can the frame rate go?

The main cortical branches and the larger microvessels stay visible all the way down to 2 FPS. Finer capillaries blur as the frame rate drops. Conventional ULM run on the same sparse data doesn’t produce a continuous network at all.

At 2 FPS the reconstruction uses 341 frames, against 170,400 for the full ULM map: about a 500× reduction in data.

The resolution cost

We measured vessel width as full width at half maximum (−3 dB) across five vessels:

Method Vessel width, µm (mean ± std)
Conventional ULM (1,000 FPS) 34.9 ± 30.5
VascFlexMap, 50 FPS 108.8 ± 43.3
VascFlexMap, 25 FPS 115.0 ± 35.9
VascFlexMap, 15 FPS 127.3 ± 24.7
VascFlexMap, 2 FPS 110.9 ± 15.2

Vessels come out about 3× wider than in ULM. That’s the honest price of working from so little data. Interestingly, width barely depends on frame rate between 50 and 2 FPS, and the spread actually narrows at 2 FPS. This fits the idea that the network leans on its learned vessel prior: fewer frames make the map less detailed, not less consistent.

How many frames do you need?

We also varied how many of the final frames are used, at a fixed frame rate.

Informative maps appear with roughly 200 to 2,200 final frames, and end-to-end reconstruction takes 28 to 133 seconds on one GPU. That’s minutes instead of hours, from data a standard scanner could record.

Where it fits, and its limits

I think of VascFlexMap as a first look, not a replacement for ULM. A quick, low-resolution perfusion map can show whether perfusion is present, where the main branches are, and where a slow, high-fidelity ULM scan would be worth doing.

The limitations are real:

  • Wider vessels. About 3–3.6× broader than ULM, so it can’t measure capillary sizes.
  • No flow information. The output is a static probability map. ULM’s tracks also give flow speed and direction; this doesn’t.
  • Motion-free data only. PALA comes from an anaesthetised, fixed rat brain. Breathing and heartbeat motion in a patient are an open question.
  • A strong prior cuts both ways. Training on noise inputs makes the network robust, but it also means it could draw “typical” vessels where the data are weak. Testing on unusual vascular anatomy, such as tumours, is an important next step.

Takeaway

ULM’s insight is that you can beat the resolution limit by accumulating many sparse observations. VascFlexMap asks how far a learned prior can stand in for some of those observations. On this data, the answer is: far enough to recover the vessel tree from 2 FPS and a few hundred frames, as long as you accept vessels about three times wider. For a clinical scanner that can’t do 1,000 FPS, that’s a trade worth having.

This line of work is also covered by an Indian patent on which I’m an equal first inventor: A System and Method for Super-Resolution Ultrasound Reconstruction with Representation Learning on Sparse Data (Application No. 202521001823, filed January 2025, published February 2026).

Status: manuscript in preparation.

My role

  • Co-author of the manuscript (equal-contribution first authors are Ruchika Dhawan and Mihir Agarwal).
  • Contributed to the ISTU 2024 hybrid attention-based U-Net on sparse ULM data that preceded this work.
  • Equal first inventor on a published Indian patent from this line of work: A System and Method for Super-Resolution Ultrasound Reconstruction with Representation Learning on Sparse Data (Application No. 202521001823, published Feb 2026).
entry.summary: VascFlexMap: skipping microbubble localization entirely, and mapping brain microvasculature from sparse 2–50 FPS ultrasound with up to 500x less data than ULM.

entry.title: Closing the Early-Stage Blind Spot in Histotripsy Monitoring with Dice-Focal Loss

link.title: Closing the Early-Stage Blind Spot in Histotripsy Monitoring with Dice-Focal Loss

entry.content:
Problem. Histotripsy destroys tissue with cavitation bubble clouds, and B-mode ultrasound is the only real-time way to watch it. A prior ResNet-18 model was nearly blind during early treatment: Dice below 20% for fewer than 500 pulses.
Approach. Treat it as semantic segmentation, train with a combined Dice + Focal loss to handle severe class imbalance, and benchmark six modern architectures on the same data as the prior work.
Result. EfficientNet-B0 U-Net with Dice-Focal loss reaches mean IoU 0.838 and global accuracy 0.968 (prior: 0.765 / 0.956) with only 7.9M parameters, about 13.5 ms per image on an A100.

Histotripsy is one of the more striking ideas in therapeutic ultrasound. Instead of heating tissue, it fires microsecond pulses with very high peak negative pressure into a target and creates a cloud of cavitation bubbles that mechanically liquefies it. No heat, no ionizing radiation, and no heat-sink problem near blood vessels. The catch is that you need to know what you have destroyed. This post is about the part of that problem I worked on at the MUSE Lab (IIT Gandhinagar): segmenting the ablation zone from B-mode ultrasound, and in particular, why our models first failed exactly when the clinician cares most.

The problem: you cannot see the lesion

Histotripsy systems are usually paired with B-mode imaging for targeting. But the lesion’s appearance changes over the treatment. Early on, the bubble cloud shows up as a hyperechoic region; later, once tissue is fragmented, it becomes hypoechoic. In between, contrast is low and the region is speckled. Right now, confirming that an ablation worked often means going to CT or MRI, which adds time, cost and complexity. A model that outlines the ablated region directly on the live ultrasound image could close that loop.

A previous paper from our collaborators (Miao et al., IEEE TBME 2024) trained a ResNet-18 with transfer learning to do this. It worked reasonably overall, but it had a blind spot: the Dice similarity coefficient was below 20% for fewer than 500 applied pulses. The early frames are precisely when you would want to adjust a treatment, so this was the gap we wanted to close.

Setting up a fair comparison

I wanted every number in our study to be comparable to the earlier work, so we used the same experimental data. The data come from agarose phantoms containing a red-blood-cell layer. When histotripsy ablates the layer, it changes color, so a synchronized camera records ground truth while the ultrasound probe records B-mode images. Otsu-thresholding the optical images and co-registering them with fiducial markers gives masks in ultrasound coordinates.

The dataset is small: nine experimental runs, 880 ultrasound images (an image every 20 pulses). One run is held out for validation, and four fully independent phantoms (400 images) are used only for testing. That is the same test set as the prior paper. Small data has a real consequence: you need to be careful with leakage, so we used a leave-one-dataset-out strategy and dropped a few timestamps to avoid overlap.

Before changing anything, I re-implemented the ResNet-18 baseline in PyTorch. Its global accuracy (0.954 vs 0.956) and weighted IoU (0.916 vs 0.916) landed very close to the published numbers, which gave me confidence that later gains were not an artifact of a different pipeline.

What we tried

We evaluated six architectures spanning 3.2M to 58.6M parameters:

  • ResNet-18 (the baseline, adapted to segmentation)
  • MobileNetV3 LR-ASPP
  • SegFormer-B0
  • MobileViT-v2 with a U-Net decoder
  • EfficientNet-B0 U-Net
  • DeepLabV3 with a ResNet-101 backbone, as a high-capacity reference

All were fine-tuned from public pretrained weights and trained with identical settings (AdamW, learning rate \(10^{-3}\), cosine annealing with warm restarts, batch size 16, 128x512 input) so architecture was the only variable.

The more important variable turned out to be the loss.

Why Dice alone struggles here

In early frames, ablated pixels are a minuscule fraction of the image. Cross-entropy is swamped by background. Dice loss helps with imbalance, but when the foreground is a few faint pixels its gradients are noisy, and the model can score decently by predicting almost nothing. We added a focal term:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Focal}}(p_t) = -\alpha_t (1-p_t)^{\gamma} \log(p_t), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{Focal}}\]

with \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\gamma = 2\). The \((1-p_t)^\gamma\) factor shrinks the loss on pixels the model already classifies confidently, which in this problem is nearly all of the background. What is left is the hard, sparse foreground. Both terms are weighted 1.0.

What worked

The loss change was the single most consistent improvement. For every architecture we tested, Dice-Focal beat Dice alone: ResNet-18 went from DSC 0.757 to 0.791, and EfficientNet-B0 from 0.748 to 0.831.

On the 400 independent test images, the headline comparison is:

Method Global Acc. Mean IoU Weighted IoU
Prior ResNet-18 0.956 0.765 0.916
EfficientNet-B0 + Dice-Focal 0.968 0.838 0.939
DeepLabV3 + Dice-Focal 0.960 0.812 0.927

The pulse-dependence curve is the one I care about most. With the prior training setup, the baseline sits near zero below 500 pulses. Both EfficientNet-B0 and DeepLabV3 with Dice-Focal loss rise steeply from around 300 pulses and plateau at about 0.83 and 0.88 respectively, versus 0.63 for the baseline.

The area plot shows a second, quieter failure of the baseline: it over-predicts the ablated area throughout treatment, around 130 mm\(^2\) even when the true ablation is zero (Pearson r = 0.61, MAE 49.8 mm\(^2\)). EfficientNet-B0 tracks the true area from the outset (r = 0.967, MAE 5.98 mm\(^2\)), and DeepLabV3 is tightest (r = 0.978, MAE 5.03 mm\(^2\)). For a clinician, an area estimate that is right is more useful than a pretty mask.

The small model wins

The pleasant surprise was efficiency. EfficientNet-B0 U-Net has 7.9M parameters, 7.4 times fewer than DeepLabV3 (58.6M), and still had the better Dice (0.831 vs 0.802) and mean IoU. It runs at roughly 13.5 ms per image on an A100. DeepLabV3’s strength is the area-tracking correlation, which we attribute to its multi-scale atrous convolutions. As a reference upper bound it is useful; as a deployable model, the small U-Net makes more sense.

What did not work, or is not solved

  • Bigger was not better. The 58.6M-parameter DeepLabV3 did not beat EfficientNet-B0 on Dice, and the lightweight options (MobileNetV3, MobileViT-v2) did not either.
  • Dice-only EfficientNet-B0 was unstable. Its DSC looked moderate at 0.748, but its area correlation was negative (r = -0.668). That is a good reminder that a single overlap metric can hide a model that is not tracking the physical quantity you care about.
  • Under about 100 pulses is still hard. The class imbalance there is extreme and we did not solve it. Targeted augmentation is the next thing I would try.
  • Phantoms are not tissue. Everything is in-vitro agarose. Ex-vivo and in-vivo data will change speckle statistics and annotation quality; semi-supervised or domain-adaptation methods may reduce the labeling burden.
  • Labels are noisy. Ground truth comes from thresholded optical images, and annotation variability was a recurring challenge noted in the project.

Takeaways

  1. When the signal you care about is a sparse minority of pixels, change the loss before you change the architecture. Of all the changes we made, this was the most consistent.
  2. Re-implement the baseline and match the published numbers first. It is tedious, but it is what makes the comparison credible.
  3. Track the physical quantity (here, lesion area) and not only an overlap score.
  4. A 7.9M-parameter model that matches or beats a 58.6M one is the more interesting result for a system that has to run beside a therapy device.

My role

  • First-listed contributor on the repo and manuscript; worked on the six-architecture benchmark and the Combined Dice-Focal loss.
  • Re-implemented the prior ResNet-18 baseline in PyTorch and checked that it closely reproduces the published metrics (global accuracy 0.954 vs 0.956; weighted IoU 0.916 vs 0.916).
  • Worked in the MUSE Lab at IIT Gandhinagar with Prof. Himanshu Shekhar; experimental data came from collaborators at the University of Chicago (Prof. Kenneth Bader).

Links

  • Code: ShreyansJain04/BubbleSegmentation
entry.summary: How a loss-function change, more than a bigger network, fixed segmentation of sparse bubble clouds in B-mode ultrasound.

entry.title: Detecting AI-Generated Images at 32x32: Our Adobe Challenge at Inter-IIT 13.0

link.title: Detecting AI-Generated Images at 32x32: Our Adobe Challenge at Inter-IIT 13.0

entry.content:
Problem. Adobe Research’s Inter-IIT 13.0 problem: detect AI-generated images in a 32x32 dataset (CIFAKE plus GAN, diffusion and Adobe Firefly images), then explain why an image looks synthetic.
Approach. A LeViT-192 classifier on Neighboring Pixel Relationship (NPR) features, pretrained on 4M GenImage samples, fine-tuned on CIFAKE with frequency-noise and blur augmentation and focal loss. A zero-shot Ovis 1.6 VLM then names and describes artifacts in flagged images.
Result. 99.21% accuracy on CIFAKE (F1 0.9869), the highest accuracy among competing teams. Silver Medal at Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13.0, IIT Bombay.

Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13.0, held at IIT Bombay, included a computer-vision problem statement from Adobe Research: detect AI-generated images, then explain why an image looks fake. I led our team (Team 64, IIT Gandhinagar), which I put together from the ML Club, and we won a Silver Medal with the highest detection accuracy among all IITs. This post goes through what we built, why each piece was there, and, with some hindsight, which parts held up.

The code is on GitHub.

The two tasks, and the catch

  1. Detection. Classify 32×32 images as real or AI-generated. The fakes came from several GANs, diffusion models and Adobe Firefly. CIFAKE was provided for development, with a ResNet-50 baseline in the problem statement.
  2. Explanation. For each image flagged as fake, name the artifacts that give it away and describe them briefly.

The catch is the resolution. At 32×32 an image is 1,024 pixels. Most of the cues people use to spot a fake (garbled text, odd hands, inconsistent reflections) simply aren’t visible. That pushed us towards signals that survive at tiny sizes, and it’s also why the explanation task turned out to be much harder than it looked.

Detection: three ideas that stacked

1. A small, fast backbone

We benchmarked two model families on CIFAKE (50,000 training and 10,000 test images):

  • LeViT, a hybrid that uses convolutions early to shrink the image, then transformer attention on the smaller feature maps. It’s built for fast inference.
  • EfficientNet, a CNN that scales depth, width and resolution together.

We also plotted parameter count against inference time, because a detector is only useful if it’s cheap to run on every uploaded image.

On their own, the backbones were close. EfficientNet-B0 led at 98.47%, LeViT-128 scored 97.14%, and the bigger LeViT-192 actually did worse at 95.87%. A larger model didn’t help on 32×32 inputs, so the gains had to come from what we fed the model and how we trained it.

2. Looking where generators leave fingerprints: NPR

Almost every image generator, GAN or diffusion, builds its output by up-sampling: it produces a small feature map and repeatedly enlarges it. Up-sampling copies or interpolates values, so neighbouring output pixels end up more correlated than they would be in a real photo. That correlation is a fingerprint.

Neighboring Pixel Relationships (NPR), from Tan et al. (CVPR 2024), turns that into a feature. Shrink the image by 2× and enlarge it back with nearest-neighbour interpolation, then take the difference:

\[\mathrm{NPR}(x) = x - \mathrm{up}_{2\times}\!\big(\mathrm{down}_{2\times}(x)\big)\]

Within each 2×2 block, this measures how each pixel differs from its block’s reference pixel. Natural images and up-sampled images have different statistics here. Because NPR works in the pixel domain, not the frequency domain, it generalises across generators well: the original paper reports results on images from 28 different generators, beating earlier methods by 11.6%.

Here is NPR computed on two of the images our model flagged as fake:

Feeding NPR into the classifier was the single biggest jump: LeViT-128 went from 97.14% to 98.88%.

3. Pretraining at scale, then robustness

Accuracy on clean CIFAKE isn’t the real goal. Real images get compressed, resized and blurred, and the hidden test set could include generators we hadn’t seen. So we did three things:

  • Pretrain on GenImage. We pretrained LeViT-192 for real-versus-fake on 4 million images subsampled from GenImage, resized to 32×32 and covering the ImageNet-1K classes across many generators. Then we fine-tuned on CIFAKE, whose classes match the CIFAR-10 evaluation set.
  • Augment like the real world. JPEG compression and blur, plus frequency noise: small random perturbations to the image’s Fourier components, simulating the high-frequency changes that resampling and re-encoding cause.
  • Focal loss. This down-weights examples the model already gets right and concentrates training on hard ones:
\[\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha (1 - p_t)^\gamma \log(p_t) + 0.6 \cdot \mathrm{BCE}, \qquad p_t = e^{-\mathrm{BCE}}\]

Were blur and frequency noise really different augmentations, or two names for the same thing? We checked statistically by measuring how each one shifts a set of hand-crafted image features. Frequency noise significantly moved frequency-domain features such as mean frequency. Blur moved texture features: local binary pattern (LBP) histograms. Global statistics (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis) barely changed under either. So the two perturbations stress different parts of the representation, which is why we used both.

Results

Model Accuracy (%) Precision Recall F1
EfficientNet-v2-S (from scratch) 96.39 0.966 0.961 0.964
LeViT-128s 96.99 0.971 0.969 0.970
LeViT-128 97.14 0.982 0.961 0.971
LeViT-192 95.87 0.960 0.957 0.959
LeViT-128 + aug 98.08 0.983 0.979 0.981
LeViT-192 + aug 98.17 0.981 0.983 0.982
EfficientNet-B0 98.47 0.984 0.985 0.985
LeViT-128 + NPR 98.88 0.986 0.987 0.980
LeViT-192 + NPR + aug + frequency noise 99.21 0.992 0.982 0.987

Two things stand out. Augmentation alone helped the larger LeViT-192 most (95.87% → 98.17%): the bigger model had been overfitting, and robustness training gave it something useful to learn. And no single idea was enough. NPR, pretraining and augmentation each added roughly half to one point, and the final model is the one that combined them all.

Explanation: what the vision-language model actually did

The setup

No dataset pairs fake images with labelled artifacts, so we couldn’t train an explainer. We used Ovis 1.6 (Gemma2-9B), an open vision-language model, zero-shot. Every image the detector flagged was sent to Ovis with one prompt listing candidate artifacts by category (anatomy, texture, lighting, geometry, mechanical parts and so on), asking for a structured reply of {artifact: explanation}.

The outputs read well. For the airplane above, Ovis said the edges were “blurred, lacking clear definition” and the window reflections were “not natural”. For the cat, it pointed to “texture bleeding between adjacent regions”. We put examples like these in our final report.

Looking back: auditing all 94 explanations

Reading the full output file again for this post, I counted what the model actually returned across all 94 flagged images:

  • It reported an average of 37 artifacts per image, with a minimum of 9 and a maximum of 62. For a 1,024-pixel image, that isn’t a diagnosis, it’s a checklist.
  • “Unrealistic specular highlights” was reported for every single image, including ones with no shiny surfaces.
  • In 9% of explanations (317 of 3,466), the model contradicted itself, saying an artifact was present while stating its subject wasn’t. Real examples: “Metallic surface artifacts: there are no metallic surfaces, but the artifacts suggest a digital manipulation”, and “incorrect wheel geometry” or “misaligned body panels” on images with no vehicle.

The pattern is clear: when a prompt lists candidate artifacts, the VLM tends to confirm the list instead of checking it. At 32×32 there’s very little visual evidence to anchor it, so it fills the gap with plausible-sounding text. The explanations sounded right, but they weren’t evidence.

What I’d do instead

  • Ask for absence explicitly. Ask about one artifact at a time, with “not present” as an equally valid answer, and score the model’s confidence.
  • Ground explanations in the detector. Use attribution maps from the classifier, or NPR residual maps like the ones above, to show where the evidence is, then ask the VLM to describe only those regions.
  • Upscale before explaining. A super-resolved view gives the VLM more to work with, though it adds its own artifacts.
  • Build a small labelled set. Even a few hundred images with human-marked artifacts would let you measure explanation precision instead of guessing it.

What remained open

  • Resolution. At 32×32, subtle artifacts are invisible. Working at full resolution would need much more compute and probably a stronger detector.
  • Generator coverage. Accuracy depends on how varied the training generators are. Generalising to unseen generators is the hard problem.
  • Continuing with Adobe. After the competition we continued working with Adobe Research on out-of-distribution generalisation, exploring adversarial training, jigsaw-style self-supervised learning and continual learning.

Takeaway

The detection side taught me that, at tiny resolutions, the right representation matters more than model size. NPR targets the one fingerprint every up-sampling generator leaves, and it beat simply scaling the backbone. The explanation side taught me something more uncomfortable: a fluent explanation is not a correct one. If I did it again, I would measure the explainer as carefully as the detector.

My role

  • Team lead: assembled the team from the ML Club, set the technical direction, and built the LeViT + NPR detection framework and the frequency augmentation pipeline.
  • Continued with Adobe Research on out-of-distribution robustness, exploring adversarial training, jigsaw-style self-supervised learning and continual learning.
entry.summary: How LeViT, Neighboring Pixel Relationships and frequency-noise augmentation reached 99.21% on CIFAKE, and an honest look at what a zero-shot VLM's artifact explanations were really worth.

entry.title: WavShadow: Teaching a Shadow Remover Where to Look

link.title: WavShadow: Teaching a Shadow Remover Where to Look

entry.content:
Problem. Shadow segmentation and removal are hard in complex real-world scenes, and existing removal models converge slowly.
Approach. Improve ShadowFormer with Masked Autoencoder (MAE) priors trained on Places2 and Fast Fourier Convolution (FFC) blocks, add Haar wavelet features for edges and multi-scale analysis, and use a modified SAM Adapter for segmentation.
Result. State-of-the-art results on the DESOBA dataset with faster convergence and better removal quality. Accepted at ICVGIP 2024.

Removing a shadow from a photo sounds like a brightness fix: find the dark region and lighten it. Anyone who has tried knows it isn’t. Shadows have soft edges that fade over many pixels, they fall across textures that must survive the fix, and the region under a shadow has lost information that has to be guessed back. Get the mask slightly wrong and you leave a halo. Get the relighting wrong and you leave a patch that’s too flat or the wrong colour.

WavShadow is our answer to this, published at ICVGIP 2024. It was a four-person project at IIT Gandhinagar with Viraj Vekaria, Karan Gandhi and Aadya Arora (all equal contribution), advised by Prof. Shanmuganathan Raman. This post explains the design choices and what they bought us.

Two problems, not one

Shadow removal is really two problems:

  1. Where is the shadow? A segmentation problem: produce a mask.
  2. What would the scene look like without it? A restoration problem: relight the masked region so it matches the lit region around it.

Most strong removal models, including ShadowFormer, which we built on, assume a mask is given. In benchmarks that’s often the ground-truth mask. Real images don’t come with one. So our pipeline produces its own mask first, then removes the shadow using that mask.

Why DESOBA, not just ISTD

The standard benchmark, ISTD, is mostly simple scenes: one shadow cast on a fairly uniform surface. We wanted to test on DESOBA, which pairs shadows with the objects that cast them in cluttered real-world scenes: people, poles and bags on grass, pavement and courts. Shadows there cross several textures and overlap with object edges, which is exactly where mask errors and halos show up.

Part 1: finding the shadow, with wavelets

For segmentation we started from the Segment Anything Model (SAM), which already has a very general sense of “what is an object region”. SAM wasn’t trained for shadows, so we used a SAM adapter: small trainable modules inserted into a frozen SAM that inject task-specific features. Our change was what we fed the adapter: Haar wavelet features.

A one-level Haar transform splits an image into four half-resolution bands. Each 2×2 block of pixels \(a, b, c, d\) becomes:

\[LL = \tfrac{a+b+c+d}{2}, \quad LH = \tfrac{a+b-c-d}{2}, \quad HL = \tfrac{a-b+c-d}{2}, \quad HH = \tfrac{a-b-c+d}{2}\]

LL is a blurred copy of the image; LH, HL and HH respond to horizontal, vertical and diagonal changes. Here is that decomposition applied to one of the DESOBA images from our results:

We chose Haar for three reasons:

  • It’s nearly free. Additions and subtractions on 2×2 blocks, with no learned parameters.
  • It keeps sharp discontinuities. Haar’s basis functions are step functions, so a hard shadow edge produces a strong, localised response instead of being smeared.
  • It’s multi-scale. Applied repeatedly, it separates coarse brightness changes from fine edges. That helps tell a soft penumbra, which spreads over many pixels, from a hard cast edge.

The figure also shows the catch: wavelets react to any edge, including texture. On their own they would make a poor shadow detector. As extra input to a model that already understands regions, they tell it precisely where intensity jumps, and the model works out which jumps are shadow boundaries.

Part 2: removing it, with priors and global context

ShadowFormer is a transformer-based removal network whose Shadow-Interaction Module uses the mask to let shadowed pixels attend to lit pixels with similar context. It’s strong but slow to train. We made two changes.

Masked-autoencoder (MAE) priors. An MAE is trained to fill in large masked regions of an image. One trained on Places2, a big dataset of scenes, has a good sense of what a pavement, a lawn or a wall usually looks like. We give it the shadowed image and our predicted mask and take its output \(I'\) as a rough guess of the shadow-free scene. That guess is concatenated with the input to ShadowFormer. The removal network no longer starts from nothing inside the shadow: it starts from a plausible reconstruction and refines it.

Fast Fourier Convolutions (FFC). Ordinary convolutions see only a small neighbourhood. FFC blocks, popularised by the LaMa inpainting model, add a branch that works in the frequency domain, so each output depends on the whole image. Relighting a shadow correctly needs global context (what’s the lighting and colour of the lit part of this surface?), so we put FFC blocks inside ShadowFormer’s shadow-interaction module.

Results

The predicted masks follow the ground truth closely, including thin structures like the strap shadow in the first row. The removed shadows blend into the surrounding texture without obvious halos.

Quantitatively (PSNR and SSIM higher is better, RMSE lower is better):

Model Dataset Shadow PSNR Shadow RMSE Non-shadow RMSE All PSNR All RMSE
ShadowFormer (L) DESOBA 37.46 13.00 0.311 36.29 0.963
MAE + FFC + ShadowFormer DESOBA 37.96 10.90 0.208 36.67 0.753
MAE + ShadowFormer DESOBA 37.14 13.55 0.208 36.67 0.886
ShadowFormer (L) ISTD 37.07 4.82 4.42 30.58 4.82
MAE + FFC + ShadowFormer ISTD 36.78 7.60 4.45 30.33 4.90

Three things stand out:

  • On DESOBA, the full model wins on every metric. The biggest gain is inside the shadow, where RMSE falls from 13.0 to 10.9 (about 16%). That’s the region the MAE prior was meant to help.
  • FFC matters. MAE alone improves the whole image but not the shadow region. Adding FFC’s global context is what fixes the shadow interior.
  • On ISTD it’s roughly a tie, with vanilla ShadowFormer slightly ahead. ISTD’s simple scenes leave little for a scene prior or global context to add. That’s consistent with our reason for focusing on DESOBA.

The clearest practical win is training speed. With the MAE prior and FFC blocks, the removal network converged in about 250 epochs instead of about 450 for the original, a 45% saving in training time, for equal or better quality. Adding wavelet features also made the SAM adapter converge faster and segment better, though we didn’t measure that speed-up as precisely. A good prior means the network has less to learn from scratch.

What I’d do differently

  • Train jointly. The SAM adapter and the removal network were trained separately, so mask errors aren’t corrected by the removal loss. An end-to-end version could learn masks that are best for removal, not just for segmentation.
  • Learn the wavelets. Haar is a fixed, hand-picked basis. Learnable or multi-level wavelets could separate shadow edges from texture better than the single level we used.
  • Run proper ablations on segmentation. Our numbers isolate the removal changes well, but the wavelet contribution to mask quality deserves its own metrics, such as balanced error rate.

Takeaway

None of the parts are exotic: a fixed wavelet transform, a pretrained segmenter, a pretrained inpainter, and a convolution with a global receptive field. The lesson for me was about where to put prior knowledge. Each component handles one thing the base model was weak at (sharp edges, region understanding, scene plausibility, global lighting), and together they make a strong model train faster and do better on the hard cases.

Links: Paper (arXiv)

My role

  • First author; all four authors (with Viraj Vekaria, Karan Gandhi and Aadya Arora) contributed equally.
entry.summary: How Haar wavelets, a SAM adapter, masked-autoencoder priors and Fourier convolutions made ShadowFormer converge in about half the epochs on hard real-world shadows (ICVGIP 2024).

entry.title: Building a Real-Time, Two-Stage Streak Suppressor for Therapy-Guidance Ultrasound

link.title: Building a Real-Time, Two-Stage Streak Suppressor for Therapy-Guidance Ultrasound

entry.content:
Problem. When an imaging probe runs during focused-ultrasound therapy (HIFU, histotripsy), interference from the therapy field paints bright streaks across the B-mode image, hiding exactly what the clinician needs to watch.
Approach. A two-stage pipeline: a multi-channel U-Net segments the streaks, and a Fourier-attention U-Net inpaints the masked regions. Training data comes from synthetic streaks with Gaussian intensity modulation across several ultrasound domains.
Result. Real-time inference at more than 440 FPS and a +13.7 dB gain in reconstruction quality (CV figures). Presented at ISTU 2024 and the IEEE South Asian Ultrasonics Symposium (SAUS) 2024.

When a focused-ultrasound therapy such as HIFU or histotripsy runs, the same time-sensitive question hangs over every treatment: what is happening in the tissue right now? B-mode imaging is the live window, but the therapy field interferes with the imaging field, and the resulting image gets streaks. This post is the story of the work I did with Mihir Agarwal, Ruchika Dhawan, Nishita Mistry and Prof. Himanshu Shekhar at the MUSE Lab (IIT Gandhinagar) between December 2023 and July 2024 to remove them fast enough to be used during therapy.

The constraint: it has to be live

Plenty of ways to clean up an ultrasound image exist if you can afford offline processing. Therapy guidance cannot. If a method is slower than the imaging frame rate, it is useless for the thing it is meant to guide. So from the start the design target was not just “good image quality” but “good quality at a speed no longer a bottleneck”. That one requirement shaped almost every choice below.

The problem has two different halves

Streaks are mostly vertical, bright, thin features that cover some of the image and leave the rest intact. Fixing them involves two different questions:

  1. Where are the streaks? A detection problem, answered by a binary mask.
  2. What should be there instead? An inpainting problem: fill in the masked pixels plausibly from the context.

A single network can try to do both, but each half has a different character. Detection is a segmentation task that U-Nets handle well. Inpainting is about reconstructing missing structure, where frequency-domain information is useful because the streak’s periodic, vertical structure is easy to describe in Fourier space. Keeping the stages separate also means the second network is only asked to fill in masked regions rather than reinterpret the whole image.

First attempt: U-Net plus diffusion

Our first version, presented at the IEEE South Asian Ultrasonics Symposium 2024, paired a U-Net with a diffusion model. The U-Net uses skip connections to find streaks, and the diffusion model, used with text-prompt conditioning, does the inpainting. The initial findings were encouraging: an SNR improvement of 6.0 +/- 3.4 dB, IoU 0.698 for the segmentation, and fast model convergence that hinted at real-time potential. But the abstract itself flags the open questions: validation on diverse datasets and performance optimization were future work.

An iterative sampling process is intrinsically heavier than one forward pass, so for a >440 FPS target a feed-forward restoration network is the natural direction.

The two-stage pipeline

The version in the repository, Fourier-StreakNet, has these parts:

  • Streak segmentation. A multi-channel U-Net (the repository also has a variant using a frequency-domain notch filter) outputs a streak mask.
  • Restoration. A U-Net with Fourier attention layers inpaints the masked regions. The attention operates on frequency-domain features, which is where streak structure is concentrated.
  • Evaluation. The toolkit reports IoU and Dice for the mask, and PSNR and signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) for the restored images.

On the CV-reported measurements, the full pipeline runs at over 440 FPS and improves reconstruction by 13.7 dB.

The data problem and the synthetic-streak fix

The biggest practical obstacle was data. You rarely have a perfectly clean twin of an image that was streaked. Our fix was to manufacture the pairs. We isolated images that had no streaks, augmented them to increase the dataset size, and then added random streaks using heuristic functions. Because we create the streaks, we know exactly where they are, so the exact mask for training the segmentation U-Net comes for free, and the clean original is the restoration target. We then split the result into training and validation sets.

The streak intensity profile mattered. Real streaks are not uniform bars, so we modulated their intensity with Gaussian profiles, and generated data across several ultrasound domains to encourage robust generalization instead of overfitting to a single imaging setup.

Honest caveats

  • Numbers vary by stage of the work. The SAUS abstract reports 6.0 +/- 3.4 dB for the early U-Net plus diffusion system, while the later two-stage pipeline is reported at +13.7 dB. These are different systems and should not be compared directly.
  • Synthetic is not real. A model trained on synthetic streaks can only be as good as the synthetic generator. The gap to real interference patterns is the main risk, which is why the abstract’s “validate on diverse datasets” remains the key next step.
  • Speed is for the pipeline as measured, not a clinical guarantee. Integrating with a live therapy system is another engineering step.

Lessons

  1. Decompose by what each part is good at. Detection and inpainting are different problems; separating them let each network stay small and fast.
  2. Let the speed requirement drive architecture early. Iterative sampling is inherently heavier than a single forward pass, which matters when the target is real time.
  3. When you lack paired data, build the generator carefully. The quality of your synthetic degradation model is the ceiling on what the restoration network learns.
  4. Report numbers with their context. Three systems, three sets of metrics; tie each to a source.

Key numbers

Quantity Value Source
Inference speed (two-stage pipeline) more than 440 FPS CV
Reconstruction improvement +13.7 dB CV
Streak segmentation IoU (initial U-Net + diffusion study) 0.698 SAUS 2024 abstract

My role

  • Designed and implemented the two-stage framework (multi-channel U-Net segmentation, Fourier-attention U-Net inpainting).
  • Built the synthetic streak generator (Gaussian intensity modulation) and the training data pipeline.
  • First author on the ISTU 2024 abstract (Taipei) and co-author on the SAUS 2024 paper; poster linked above.
  • Equal first inventor on the published Indian patent A Real-Time Ultrasound Image Processing System and a Method Thereof (Application No. 202621026094, published Apr 2026).

entry.title: Teaching Machine Learning Through Interactive Apps

link.title: Teaching Machine Learning Through Interactive Apps

entry.content:
Problem. Machine learning algorithms are hard to understand from equations alone.
Approach. For each concept, write a Quarto blog post with from-scratch code and build a Streamlit app where the reader can change parameters and watch the algorithm run. Done as a CS299 project advised by Prof. Nipun Batra.
Result. More than a dozen live blogs and Streamlit apps covering optimization, information theory and probability. The gallery below has the highlights.

Equations are a poor first contact with an algorithm. You can stare at the Adam update for an hour and still not know what changing \(\beta_2\) does to the path of a ball rolling down a loss surface. In a CS299 project advised by Prof. Nipun Batra, Vannsh Jani, Viraj Vekaria and I (with Kishan Ved on several topics) tried a different route: for each concept, write a blog post with from-scratch code, and build a small app so the reader can poke at it. This post collects what we built, what broke, and what we would do again.

The recipe

Each topic followed the same loop:

  1. Learn the concept well enough to implement it with NumPy only.
  2. Write a Quarto blog post: motivation, maths, code, static plots.
  3. Decide what the reader should be able to change, and expose exactly that in a Streamlit app.
  4. Check the app against a trusted implementation.

Step 3 is the interesting one. A good app has two or three controls, not twelve. For the optimizer demo the controls are the optimizer, the learning rate, momentum and the starting point. Everything else is fixed so that the effect of each knob is legible.

Optimizers: first lessons in being slow

Our first optimizer app redrew the loss curve after every epoch so the path would animate. It was unusable: plotting dominated the runtime and, worse, you only saw the final state because the screen refreshed too late. The fix was boring. Store the iterates in a list, plot once at the end, and give up the live animation. Later, a “Next Step” button on a contour plot restored the sense of motion by letting the reader advance the optimizer one step at a time:

\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \alpha\,\hat m_t / (\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon)\]

Seeing momentum overshoot a narrow valley and swing back teaches more than the paragraph describing it. We also added a one-dimensional function with a saddle, a local minimum and a global minimum, with a slider over learning rates that plays a video of Adam’s path. Small learning rates get stuck; large ones skip the basin.

As a sanity check we contributed from-scratch optimizers to the open-source wimpyML library and compared them against PyTorch. On MNIST, our RMSProp reached 97.11% test accuracy versus 97.31% for torch.optim.RMSprop, with nearly the same training time (about 115.7 s versus 113.3 s for 10 iterations). Matching a reference implementation is what lets you trust an explanatory app.

Information theory: watching a tree grow

For Huffman coding, Kishan and I wrote the blog around a min-heap: repeatedly pop the two least frequent symbols, merge them, push the parent back. The app shows both the heap and the tree at each step, so a reader sees why frequent symbols end up near the root. The same machinery reappears in JPEG, where the quantized DCT coefficients are turned into (run, size) pairs and then Huffman-coded; a second app shows that encoding and decoding, and a Colab notebook walks through the whole pipeline: RGB to YCbCr, chroma subsampling, DCT, quantization, entropy coding.

Vannsh took on the neighbouring topics: Shannon-Fano coding, noisy channel coding (with plots of bit error probability against message length and rate), mutual information, and SIREN, which stores an audio clip or an image as the weights of a small network with sinusoidal activations. SIRENs reconstruct beautifully and compress well, but the report is honest about the catch: training on one image takes on the order of an hour, so it is not practical without further optimization.

Fisher information, Jacobians and CORDIC

My own topics were the ones where a picture changes the intuition most.

Fisher information measures how sensitive the likelihood is to a parameter \(\theta\): high information means the data pins \(\theta\) down tightly. The app lets you choose a distribution (normal, Poisson, binomial) and parameters and shows the resulting information.

Change of variables is the Jacobian determinant in

\[\iiint f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz = \iiint f(u,v,w)\,|\det J|\,du\,dv\,dw .\]
The app takes a transformation and shows how a small patch of space is stretched, which makes $$ \det J $$ feel like what it is: a local area (or volume) scale factor.

CORDIC, built with Viraj, rotates a vector toward a target angle by a sequence of shifts and adds, using no multiplications. The app draws the start vector, the current vector, a reference circle and the running sine and cosine; each press of “Next Iteration” applies one more rotation, and you can watch the red arrow close in on the blue one.

What failed, and lessons

  • Too much interactivity. Our design rule became two or three controls per app; every extra knob makes the effect of each one harder to see.
  • Speed is a feature. Our per-epoch redraw showed that slow interaction kills exploration. Precompute, cache, and plot once.
  • The blog comes first. In our view the apps work best with a written explanation that told the reader what to look for. An app without a question to answer is a toy.
  • Validate against a reference. Autodiff, optimizers and Huffman codes were all checked against PyTorch or a library before we put them in front of readers.
  • Learning is the real output. As the report notes, a lot of the early work on each task went into learning the concept before any visualization was possible.

Demo gallery

Each card opens a live app or blog. All of them are listed on the project Notion page.

Contour plots: updates after every epoch
Velocity visualization for momentum
Optimization path explorer
CORDIC algorithm
Constrained optimization (blog)
Computational graphs and autodiff (blog)

Topic App Authors

CORDIC algorithm cordic.streamlit.app Viraj and Shreyans
Change of variables (Jacobian) changeofvariables.streamlit.app Shreyans
Noisy channel coding noisychannelcoding.streamlit.app Vannsh

My role

  • Optimizers. With Viraj, built the Streamlit app comparing SGD, Adam and RMSProp, plus the contour-plot momentum demo and the velocity app.
  • Information theory. With Kishan, the Huffman coding blog and app, and a Colab walk-through of the JPEG pipeline (YCbCr, chroma subsampling, DCT, quantization, Huffman).
  • Maths concepts. Blogs and apps on Fisher information and on change of variables with the Jacobian; with Viraj, the CORDIC app.

Links

  • Full write-up: project notion page
  • Apps: Fisher information, Huffman, JPEG coding, CORDIC, change of variables, velocity viz, noisy channel coding

Thanks to Prof. Nipun Batra for the opportunity to learn machine learning this way.

from itertools import permutations
from torchvision.transforms import functional as F


def extract_patches(image, grid_size=3):
    patch_size = image.size(1) // grid_size
    patches = [F.crop(image, i, j, patch_size, patch_size)
               for i in range(0, image.size(1), patch_size)
               for j in range(0, image.size(2), patch_size)]
    return patches


def apply_permutation(patches, perm):
    return [patches[i] for i in perm]

from torch.utils.data import Dataset


class JigsawPuzzleDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, dataset, permutations):
        self.dataset = dataset
        self.permutations = permutations

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.dataset)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        image, _ = self.dataset[idx]
        perm_idx = np.random.choice(len(self.permutations))
        perm = self.permutations[perm_idx]
        shuffled_patches = apply_permutation(extract_patches(image), perm)
        # Convert list of patches to tensor
        shuffled_image = torch.stack(shuffled_patches)
        return shuffled_image, perm_idx

entry.title: Fisher Information
entry.content:
Used to find out how much information a particular random variable has about an unknown parameter. Example: If we have a coin and we want to know if it is fair or not, we can toss it 100 times and count the number of heads. If we get 100 heads, we can be pretty sure that the coin is not fair. If we get 50 heads, we can’t be sure. If we get 0 heads, we can be pretty sure that the coin is not fair. So, the number of heads gives us information about the fairness of the coin. The Fisher information is a measure of how much information a random variable has about an unknown parameter.

The math: Its defined as the variance of the score of log likelihood of a random variable. But the the partial derivative of the log-likelihood behaves similarly to a random variable, just like y. It possesses both a mean and a variance.

When the variance of this derivative is smaller, there is a higher probability that the observed value y will closely match the true mean of the probability distribution of y. In simpler terms, more information about the true mean of y is embedded within the random variable y itself. Conversely, when the variance of the partial derivative of ℓ(λ y=y) is greater, the information contained in y about its true mean diminishes.

The relationship between the information embedded in ‘y’ regarding the genuine value of a parameter θ, drawn from the assumed distribution of ‘y,’ is inversely proportional to the variance of the partial derivative concerning θ in the log-likelihood function.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

range_min = -10
range_max = 10
num_points = 20

x_values = np.linspace(range_min, range_max, num_points)

variance1 = 10
variance2 = 25

fig, ((ax1, ax2), (ax3, ax4)) = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 10))


for i, x in enumerate(x_values):
    log_likelihood1 = -0.5 * \
        np.log(2 * np.pi * variance1) - ((x - x_values) ** 2) / (2 * variance1)
    log_likelihood2 = -0.5 * \
        np.log(2 * np.pi * variance2) - ((x - x_values) ** 2) / (2 * variance2)
    score1 = (x - x_values) / variance1
    score2 = (x - x_values) / variance2

    ax1.plot(x_values, log_likelihood1, label=f"Observation Point {i+1}")
    ax2.plot(x_values, log_likelihood2, label=f"Observation Point {i+1}")
    ax3.plot(x_values, score1, label=f"Observation Point {i+1}")
    ax4.plot(x_values, score2, label=f"Observation Point {i+1}")

ax1.set_xlabel("Observation")
ax1.set_ylabel("Log-Likelihood")
ax1.set_title(f"Log-Likelihood for Variance {variance1}")
ax1.grid()
ax1.set_ylim([-10, 0])  # set y-limits

ax2.set_xlabel("Observation")
ax2.set_ylabel("Log-Likelihood")
ax2.set_title(f"Log-Likelihood for Variance {variance2}")
ax2.grid()
ax2.set_ylim([-10, 0])  # set y-limits

ax3.set_xlabel("Observation")
ax3.set_ylabel("Score")
ax3.set_title(f"Score for Variance {variance1}")
ax3.grid()
ax3.set_ylim([-3, 4])
ax4.set_xlabel("Observation")
ax4.set_ylabel("Score")
ax4.set_title(f"Score for Variance {variance2}")
ax4.grid()
ax4.set_ylim([-3, 4])

plt.show()

We see that in the case of less variance the score matrix is more varied and hence contains more information about the true mean. We can also see from the log likliehood graphs that a lower variance is showing us that most points in our sample peak at zero indicating its the true mean wheareas a higher variance does not easily tell us where the peak us.

To make it more intuitive, in our previous example if we can crudely say that when the results follow a ‘pattern’ and the results are less varied we actually have more information about the biasing.
entry.summary: A short numerical intuition for Fisher information via the score function and its variance.
